messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 76
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Hotel Manager
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 73

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Sensory Distraction: I put on loud music or TV, Thought Monitoring: constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy, Avoid Event Site: avoid site of the event
  Threat: Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home, Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
  Memory: Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
  Negative Appraisals: Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

At seventy-six, the divorced European-American hotel manager had spent forty-two years overseeing the Meridian, but a ruptured industrial solvent tank during a late-summer renovation altered the architecture of his life. The incident began with a sharp, unexpected hiss from the basement mechanical room, followed by a thick, acrid cloud that seeped through the lobby vents. Arthur remembers the taste of copper on his tongue and the way his chest tightened as the chemical fumes rolled over the marble floors. He had come to believe the air itself had turned against him. Even now, years later, he can still catch whiffs of that same solvent when he walks past certain hardware stores, an olfactory recall that brings back the full emotional intensity of the exposure without any clear picture of what occurred. His memories arrive as fragmented pieces: the hiss of the valve, the maintenance supervisor’s clipped voice, the sensation of his knees buckling, yet they never stitch together into a single coherent scene. When the emotional intensity washes over him, it does so without an accompanying image, leaving him alone with the visceral weight of the moment. As the months passed, Arthur’s body began to feel less like a reliable instrument and more like a constant signal of distress. He can no longer trust his own breathing, his pulse, or the occasional tremor in his hands. Each unfamiliar sensation remains alongside his awareness of the chemical exposure. He is on high alert when he hears unexpected or loud sounds, particularly the sharp clatter of the hotel’s pneumatic doors or the sudden ring of the telephone. When those sounds echo through the lobby, his shoulders rise instinctively, his body reacting as if he is still standing in that expanding cloud. His PCL-5 score of seventy-three mirrors what he experiences daily: his body keeps reacting as if he is still in danger, even when he is perfectly safe. His helplessness settles over him, while his thoughts continue to monitor themselves constantly. He mentally checks for any sign that he is going crazy, while the physical world around him remains unchanged. Arthur developed a narrow circle of safety. He feels on guard even inside his own home, constantly scanning the rooms for invisible drafts or lingering odors, yet he only feels truly safe in two specific places: the back of his study armchair and the edge of his bed. To keep the world at bay, he begins putting on loud music or leaving the television running at high volume, using sensory distraction to dampen the unpredictable noises. Over time, he avoids the site of the event, refusing to enter the hotel’s mechanical wing or walk the main corridors where the solvent had first breached the floor. This avoidance shapes his daily routine; he still manages the property by phone, but he ceases making the physical rounds, watching his professional life slowly recede from his direct experience. He no longer steps into the hotel, convinced that another cloud or another sound would pull him back into that initial moment. What finally brings Arthur to seek help is the quiet exhaustion of living in a state of perpetual readiness. He is most afraid that his body will betray him again, that the familiar sensations of exposure will return without warning. He is hoping, perhaps, to find a way back to the hotel without feeling trapped by the air he can no longer fully rely on.
